Jag för min del har djupt och smärtsamt gripits af Ellens uppförande; det kommer att dröja länge innan jag glömmer denna stöt!" Helmers ansigtsdrag buro syn för hwad han led i denna skärseld, men hans sjelfbeherrskning wann seger öfwer hans uppbrusande häftighet, och han swarade med ett lugn, som war wärdigt en fi- losof: „Tala icke om mig! Det är nu en öfwerflödig fråga, om fru Skovby och jag passat för hwar- andra, om hon welat hafwa mig eller jag henne — hwad mig beträffar, så war den saken icke klar, jag war långtifrån ense med mig sjelf i den- na punkt — men låtom oß endast tala om de nyförlofwade, och i afseende å dem måste jag öp- pet tillstå, att jag finner er wrede obillig. I af- färer är det er pligt att råda och wägleda den unga damen, hwars slägtinge och goda man ni är; men i hjertats angelägenheter må hon ega rätt att råda sig sjelf, och hon är ju intet barn mera." „Hm!" swarade den gamle kallt, „mycket ädel- modigt af er att taga hennes parti, men det är alltför fint uttänkt och kommer icke från hjertat. Jag kan, min själ, icke taga mitt answar så lätt. Ni är endast wan att tänka på er sjelf och era protokoller; ni har ingen föreställning om huru mycket bråk det medför att hafwa en widtutgre- nad slägt att råda och hjelpa till rätta; hwarje fadaise, som begås i familjen, sätter en klick på min ära — så tänker jag och kan icke tänka an- norlunda." Den gamle såg upp, fattade Helmer i armen och sade: „Har ni sett Harald Ström i sin upphöjelse och huru han skifwar sig på den swarta ridhästen, som Ellen förärat honom?" „Nej!" swarade Helmer med ett sjukligt leende. „Så se då upp, ty der kommer han." Knappt hade han yttrat detta, då Ajax sprang förbi dem med den lycklige fästmannen på sin rygg. Det war en wacker syn att se den kraft- fulle unge mannen på det eldiga djuret; den tätt åtknäppta rocken wisade på det fördelaktiga- ste hans smidiga wäxt, och han satt fritt och u- tan twång i sadeln. Det bittra och mörka dra- get kring hans mun war förswunnet; hans kin- der blossade och hans ögon lyste — en barett med en plym uti, en sammetskappa, ett swärd wid sidan och besporrade halfstöflor, och han skul- le hafwa warit en skön och tapper riddare att se på. Helmers skarpa blick såg det och han suckade. Ett wackert och manligt yttre, tänkte han, har i alla tider gjort ett starkare intryck på qwinno- hjertan, än andliga företräden. Mig har han förnämligast att tacka för att det engång i tiden blef wäl stäldt för honom; bara wi hade låtit honom gå! Då hade wi förmodligen haft en annan förwaltare och hela denna prostitution ha- de undwikits." „Jag har endast talat några få ord med den unge mannen", sade Helmer tankfull, „och jag har icke den ringaste föreställning om, huru detta kär- leksförhållande uppkommit; men ni känner ju ho- nom — säg mig derföre — är han en flitig kyrkogångare?" „Ja, det är han", swarade Skovby wresigt, i det han erinrade sig Ellens yttrande om Helmer sjelf rörande detta kapitel. „Tror ni då", frågade Helmer widare, „att sympati i religiöst afseende dragit dessa twå till hwarandra?       <Paragraph>
        <Line>（倫敦廿五日美聯電）英國曾以『直率之牒文』、送達希特勒、據英方發言人表示、此一牒文、內容爲希求和平、同時亦不啻爲一警吿、因於其牒文中有云、最近歐洲緊張情勢、若仍事繼續、則或致逼使英國實行全國徵兵、關於英國駐柏林大使漢德森、昨日囘返柏林時、曾隨身帶去此一牒文之報吿、英發言人、已予以證實、牒文之內容、據英官方公佈者、包括下列數點、（一）重申歐洲問題能够和平解决之信心、（二）建議羅斯福總統之和平呼籲、爲給予德國與英國合作、共謀解决歐洲問題之機會、該牒文末稱、英國希望、希特勒氏於四月廿八日答覆美總統時、不必拒絕羅斯福之建議、（三）警吿稱、德國若有任何企圖、以武力而統治歐洲時、英國將實行抵抗、</Line>

      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>黑暗的浦東</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>僞軍挨戶搜索</Line>
        <Line>公然綁架刦掠</Line>
        <Line>忠義救國軍派隊追剿</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>據浦東來人談、於本月二十四日晨四時許、塘灣南鄉翁板橋、李家圈、張家塘等處、突然到有僞軍五十餘名、首領係一翁某、開到後、卽挨戶大肆搜索、無一倖免、當時有農民茹憲章之妻、及趙秋根陳永生等、因加反抗、致遭痛毆、遍體受傷、臨行時並綁去小學教員趙學預一名、及居民趙金法、何進明、黃金海等多名、洗刼達二時後、始向塘灣方面逸去、聞已有忠義救國軍何總指揮得悉、派隊正在追剿中云、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>滬市存米</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>計六十五萬包</Line>
        <Line>評價會分四次調查</Line>
        <Line>第五次調查已着手</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>記者昨向上海市米糧評價委員會探悉、關於第四次調查存糧、蒙該會發表、總數爲六五二、四五六包、較之第三次調查、減少一、六三一包、仍以中國銀行堆棧爲第一、計一二三、六一三包、業已繕報七米業團體、及兩租界當局備查、第五次調查、亦已開始、預定下週初竣事、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>月底會較市斛</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>上海市豆米行業公會、鑒於同業所用市斛久未會斛、未免有所參差、該會爲統一起見、特經决定會較市斛、茲准於三十日上午九時、假雜糧交易所舉行、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>昌興運輸公司</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>黑幕敗露</Line>
        <Line>專假造通行證</Line>
        <Line>朱阿大判刑一年</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>虹口捕房、前在振華旅社一〇七號房間、拘獲僞造通行證之朱阿大、王士德兩名、搜得假通行證等物、解由特一法院、按朱阿大等、租賃振華房間、表面開設昌興運輸公司、實則專事出賣僞造之假通行證、赴虹口區域之證、每張售六元、往遊擊區之證、每張十元、昨晨、捕房依法正式起訴、請求懲辦、訊問後、朱阿大判處徒刑一年、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>舞女劉珍</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>求上進之志未遂</Line>
        <Line>萌厭世之念圖盡</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>舞女劉珍、今年二十歲、父已早故、隨母爲生、惟母染癖甚深、尚有一兄、爲一癱子、一家三口、純依劉珍伴舞收入、以資維持、近日珍以舞業不振、乃退而作女工、夜間則讀書、以求深造、其向上之志、有足多者、惟母則不以爲然、仍堅令其操舞業、以增收入而供其賣烟土也、珍不堪其擾、遽萌厭世之念、乃於昨日購服巨量鴉片圖盡、經家人發覺後、卽送紅十字會、迄猶在救治之中云、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>地痞搗亂米船</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>日無工部局</Line>
        <Line>敷千工人陷於失業困境</Line>
        <Line>依法訴請嚴究</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>近來內地運滬食米、大都在工部局指定之蘇州河天后宮橋昌泰交通碼頭卸貨、向有工人、包辦卸運、此項工人、總數不下千人、組織有上海市米車肩運業職業工會、近有地痞張立國張九進等、覬覦利益、糾集羽黨、專在昌泰交通及非指定之碼頭等碼頭、阻攔米船通行至工部局指定之碼頭、任意苛索、並剝削車工生計、致千百賴以生活之苦力、均陷失業困境、與之理論、反遭凶毆、聞張等贍敢如斯妄爲、其中有人在幕後主使、前由各米業公會代表該工人等、呈請當局、設法禁止、亦未見效果、該工人以此種蠻橫侵奪行爲、非特有關治安、妨礙商市、且爲法律所不許、爰有工會委聘律師爲常年法律顧問、登報警吿外、並向法院依法訴請嚴究云、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>羣玉芳武劇</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>小香閣率衆打房間</Line>
        <Line>林琳琳被打受重傷</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>五馬路羣玉坊四號書寓、爲林琳琳與小香閣、合舖房間、平日相安無事、昨日二人發生口角、事後、小香閣不甘示弱、卽糾集遊手好閒之徒數人、擁入林琳琳房間、除實行打房間外、並將林之頭部、擊穿一洞、一時血流如注、於晚間十一時許、送寶隆醫院醫治、傷勢甚重云、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>彩鳳不願隨鴉</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>王和尚誘姦少女被拘</Line>
        <Line>昨開庭案關風化禁止旁聽</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>沙遜洋行地產部高級職員王友根、有女名佩珍、年十七歲、姿色娟秀、於本月六日晨、被擺肉攤之王和尚、（廿九歲）誘至家中、實行奸汚、一連三日、其後電話通知佩珍之母前來、談判訂婚事宜、當時王母按址馳往、當由王領至大中華飯店、由該飯店經理戴步祥出面爲其談判、卒以聘金相差太遠、且因王貌不揚、致被氏所拒絕、當於本月廿三日、田王劉氏偕女佩珍、投法捕房報吿經過、旋將王和尚拘獲、昨日押送特二院刑一庭、由廖推事審理、當以案關風化、禁止旁聽、改期五月三日再訊、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>新光經理</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>控吿羅民佑等違約</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>新光大戲院經理芮慶榮、因聯華影片公司違約、近乃延律師、控吿聯華影片公司經理羅明佑、協理黎民偉、及大股東馮耿光等、請求判令連帶返還保證金一萬四千元、及未兌現之支票六千元、該案昨日傳訊、被吿均未到、經原吿代理律師陳述起訴意旨、卽宣吿審結、定四月廿七日宣判、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>甘維露化名控房東</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>充「立法委員」兼新聲半月刊編輯</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>十年前在上海會審工廨時代以外籍律師資格執行律務之</Line>
        <Line><Emphasis type="bold">甘維露</Emphasis>（英人而入華籍之者）、亦名甘德雲、最近又化名</Line>
        <Line><Emphasis type="bold">開脫衞</Emphasis>潛赴南京、充僞中華新聲半月刊編輯、兼「立法委員」、甘之家屬、則仍住趙主教路、本人常往來京滬間、最近甘寓二房東德籍老嫗羅克邱夫人、得悉甘身爲傀儡、恐發生危險、遂將電話等不准甘使用、甘乃延</Line>
        <Line><Emphasis type="bold">唐懷群</Emphasis>律師、以開脫衞之名、具狀特二院、對羅克邱夫人、提起損害倍償之訴、昨經庭訊、被吿聲稱、開脫衞者、並無此人、實係</Line>
        <Line><Emphasis type="bold">甘維露</Emphasis>之化名、他現在不是英國人、是中國人了、現在在國籍問題不能解决之前、故本案殊不能成立云云、乃諭令正式再行起訴云</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>奉賢富紳</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>身後多故</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>奉賢首富陳泊菴在滬逝世後、其妻馬文蘊與所生諸子、接踵至滬、辦竣喪務、檢點封存於箱篋中之財產契據、發覺均被妾李氏母子乾沒、於是涉訟於第二特院、初審敗訴、現尚在高三分院上訴中、最近陳馬氏與其諸子、又發覺李氏母子及其親戚楊靜廬楊耀章、（卽楊叔震）有在公共租界侵佔遺產行爲、故向第一法院提起侵佔刑事自訴、諭知兩造以本案經考慮結果、應先投民庭、請求解决繫爭之點、遂當庭裁定本件停止審判、</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>今雜事祕</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>△井波（四）</Line>
        <Line>捉刀人譔</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>冠玉以明珠之衣，一一付侍者曰：「長衣令更製新者，短衣令洗滌。」囘視明珠，已伏衾中，問之曰：「汝須進食乎？」明珠曰：「我頃觸販夫担。今猶心悸。」冠玉曰：「心如跳躍乎？」曰：「然。」冠王伸手捫之，曰：「汝體何乃亦如爲油所浸潤，使我之手，不能止於任何一處，蓋任何一處，皆凝脂也。」</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>明珠笑曰：「汝善我，特阿私所好耳，若我以手按之，則欲止於何處，卽止何處。」冠玉曰：「汝言亦未嘗不可信，我今止於一處，雖滑澤而如有吸力，我手不忍去矣。我將啓視此處爲何處。」明珠聞語，疾蒙首衾中，意謂惟此足以已羞。蒙首未幾，忽覺衾中有微光，初不知光何自來，旣而知冠玉掀衾之中部，光卽自中部來，且冠玉雙目亦炯炯然自中部來也。明珠大慚，掖衾，探首於外曰：「汝乃惡作劇，我不能堪。」</Line>
      </Paragraph>

Dutch ltr Single printed page, part of a larger volume. Good condition with some foxing and minor stains. An ordinance issued by the authorities of Friesland on April 30, 1686, concerning the prohibition of foreign 'Doyten' (coins) and their valuation.         <Line>RAKENNUSAINEKAUPPA</Line>

      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Edustalle päästetä laiwoja eikä myöskään</Line>

        <Line>ta kuitenkin näiden ohjeiden 20 kohdassa</Line>

      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>8) Poikkeuksena yleisistä säännöistä</Line>
        <Line>sallitaan pienempien rannikkolaiwojen se-</Line>
        <Line>kä hinaajalaiwojen, kuuttojen, soimain,</Line>

        <Line>ja yölläkin laskea Kronstadtin Isonsata-</Line>

        <Line>alalle, nimittäin aallonmurtajan ja sen</Line>
        <Line>palowartiolaiwan wäliin, joka seisoo sisä-</Line>
        <Line>sataman edustalla, Nikolainmajakkain</Line>
        <Line>keulamerkin eteläpuolella.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>9) Iltatykinlaukauksesta aamutykinlau-</Line>
        <Line>kaukseen asti on laiwojen ja yksityisten a-</Line>
        <Line>luksien ehdottomasti kielletty liikkumasta</Line>
        <Line>satamaedustoilla taikka pitämästä yhteyt-</Line>
        <Line>tä rannikon kanssa tahi keskenään, lukuun-</Line>
        <Line>ottamatta kuitenkaan näiden ohjeiden 20</Line>
        <Line>kohdassa mainittuja laiwoja.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Muist. Poikkeuksena tästä säännöstä</Line>
        <Line>olkoon kuitenkin pienillä purjealuksilla lu-</Line>
        <Line>pa yöllä käyttää suotuisaa tuulta päästäk-</Line>
        <Line>seen merelle.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>10) Kaikkien mereltä saapuwien kauppa-</Line>
        <Line>laiwojen on palowartiolaiwoja lähestyes-</Line>
        <Line>sään näytettäwä kutsusignaalejaan, sekä</Line>
        <Line>ilmoitettawa, mistä satamasta ne owat</Line>
        <Line>lähteneet ja mihin owat matkalla.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>11) Jos laiwojen hawaitaan tulewan</Line>
        <Line>sellaisista satamista, jotka owat julistetut</Line>
        <Line>jonkun tarttuwan taudin saastuttamiksi,</Line>
        <Line>niin on palowartiolaiwojen pysähdytettä-</Line>
        <Line>wä ne satamaedustalle päästämättä, ase-</Line>
        <Line>tettawa ne ankkuriin ja käskettäwä nos-</Line>
        <Line>tamaan karanteenilippu, jonka ohessa asi-</Line>

        <Line>le.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>12) Kaikki sellaiset rannikkolaiwat, jot-</Line>
        <Line>ka eiwät ole tullitarkastuksen alaisia, kuten</Line>
        <Line>kuutot, soimat, jahdit ja purret, owat wel-</Line>
        <Line>wolliset saapumaan tarkastusta warten</Line>
        <Line>Kronstadtin Isonsataman edustalla ole-</Line>
        <Line>wan palowartiolaiwan luo, jossa niiden</Line>

        <Line>si kunnes palowartiolaiwan wirkailijat</Line>
        <Line>ennättäwät ne wuorossaan tarkastaa.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>13) Ne 12 kohdassa mainituista ran-</Line>
        <Line>nikkolaiwoista, jotka owat saapuneet yöl-</Line>
        <Line>lä, tarkastetaan k:lo 6 aamulla.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>14) Tarpeen waatiessa owat päiwystä-</Line>

        <Line>dyttämään ja tarkastamaan jokaisen me-</Line>
        <Line>reltä saapuwan laiwan.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Pysähdyttääkseen lähestywän laiwan</Line>
        <Line>menee pysähdyttäjälaiwa sitä wastaan ta-</Line>

        <Line>lin „H D", joka kansainwälisen luettelon</Line>

        <Line>ka, jos se on yöaika, walaisee laiwan wa-</Line>
        <Line>lonheittäjällä ja samalla antaa hälyyttä-</Line>
        <Line>wiä wihellyksiä tahi myöskin waroittawan</Line>
        <Line>laukauksen tyhjällä panoksella. Näiden sig-</Line>

        <Line>tään niskoittelewaa laiwaa kohtaan ase-</Line>
        <Line>woimaa.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Muist. Ennenkuin asewoimaa ryhdy-</Line>
        <Line>tään käyttämään, annetaan siitä warot-</Line>
        <Line>tawa tieto asianomaisen laiwan laiwu-</Line>
        <Line>rille; ilman waroitusta käytetään asewoi-</Line>

        <Line>töjä suoranaisesti ja wäkiwaltaisesti ri-</Line>
        <Line>kotaan.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>15) Pidätetyn laiwan on noudatettawa</Line>
        <Line>kaikkia palowartio- tai suojeluslaiwojen</Line>
        <Line>antamia määräyksiä.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Tarpeen sattuessa owat palowartiolai-</Line>

        <Line>Muist. Erityisestä määräyksestä wie-</Line>

        <Line>tarkastusta warten Sisäpalowartiaston</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>16) Alustawan tarkastuksen jälkeen on</Line>

        <Line>sesti.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>17) Laiwa, jota kohtaan on täytynyt</Line>

        <Line>wartioitawa sitä tarkastuksen loppuun.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>18) Aluksilla, pursilla, kalastajawenheil-</Line>
        <Line>lä, soimilla ja muilla laiwoilla, jotka</Line>
        <Line>työskentelewät Kronstadtin satamaedus-</Line>
        <Line>toilla taikka harjoitlawat elinkeinoa Kron-</Line>
        <Line>stadiin linnoitusalueella, tulee olla, paitsi</Line>
        <Line>Sisäpalowartiaston antamia läkkilewyjä,</Line>
        <Line>myöskin nimitetylle laiwalle annettu lu-</Line>
        <Line>pakirja linnoituksen esikunnasta.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>19) 18 kohdassa mainittujen aluksien on</Line>
        <Line>mereltä tullessaan laskettawa siwuutta-</Line>
        <Line>miensa palowartiolaiwojen luo, näytettä-</Line>
        <Line>wä niille lupalippunsa ja saatawa niiltä</Line>
        <Line>läpikulkulupa, joka wuoksi niillä aina tu-</Line>

        <Line>waadittaessa näytettäwät suojeluslai-</Line>
        <Line>woille.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>20) Kronstadtin sataman, linnoituksen</Line>
        <Line>tykkiwäen, insinööriwiraston sekä muiden</Line>
        <Line>Kronstadtin linnawäkeen kuuluwien o-</Line>

        <Line>Muist. Pohjoista kulkuwäylää purjeh-</Line>

        <Line>tamat lupaliput.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>21) Kronstadtia lähestyessä sekä Pieta-</Line>
        <Line>riin päin mennessä on laiwojen ankarasti</Line>

        <Line>22) Kronstadtin satamaedustoilla saa-</Line>

      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>

        <Line>III) Kaikkien rannikkopurjelaiwojen,</Line>

      </Paragraph>

        <Line>c) Itäsataman edustalla: Lennätinkaa-</Line>
        <Line>pelin ulkopuolelle.</Line>

        <Line>23) Jos syystä tai toisesta katsotaan</Line>

        <Line>25) Laikokoelman II Osan 23 art:aan</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>On kuulakka juhannusaaton yö. Kuu-</Line>

      <Paragraph>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Lähenewiä askeleita kuuluu pitkin as-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Olikohan se — kuka? Työstään palaa-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Pian nousee aurinko, ajattelen. Kau-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Nyt tulla tupsahti lehti sinunkin kirje-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Samaan aikaan on waahtoawin hewo-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Koetan kuwitella olewani maalla. Kau-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Aurinko on lännen taiwaalla. Päiwälli-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Kewyessä kesäpuwussasi nähdään sinut</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Wiime sunnuntain Hels. Sanomissa on</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Paljoa huonommassa kunnossa on kui-</Line>
        <Line>tenkin Pälkäneen wanha Herran temp-</Line>
        <Line>peli. Pälkäneen wanhaan kirkkoon as-</Line>
        <Line>tuessa luulisikin tulemansa johonkuhun</Line>
        <Line>pedon luolaan, eikä ihmiswainajien le-</Line>
        <Line>popaikkaan. Käwin kesällä 1879 sitä</Line>
        <Line>katsomassa. Olipa kuolleita kiskottu</Line>
        <Line>haudoistaan, koska permanto oli koko-</Line>
        <Line>naan rewitty. Tuohon oli pieni arkku</Line>
        <Line>heitetty ja sen ruumiin jäsenet kopiste-</Line>
        <Line>tut sinne tänne! Toisessa arkussa ei ol-</Line>
        <Line>lut kantta ja siinä lepääwältä ruumiilta</Line>
        <Line>oliwat riewut rewityt hajallensa ja pää</Line>
        <Line>oli siltä poissa! Muutamassa arkussa</Line>
        <Line>taas oli nähtäwästi pappi lewännyt,</Line>
        <Line>koska joku aika sitten ruumiin leuwan</Line>
        <Line>alla papin raji oli näkynyt. Sanalla sa-</Line>
        <Line>noen: näkyi ylt'ympäri häwityksen jälkiä.</Line>
        <Line>— On kuitenkin nyt tällekin wanhalle kir-</Line>
        <Line>kolle muistoineen wihdoin rauha julis-</Line>
        <Line>tettu. — Mitä muuten kirkon keskiai-</Line>
        <Line>kuiseen rakennustapaan tulee, mainitta-</Line>
        <Line>koon ainoastaan, että sakaristo on pyö-</Line>
        <Line>riäiskaarilla holwattu 8 osaan. Ete-</Line>
        <Line>läisen porstuan (—asehuoneen, johon</Line>
        <Line>muinoin aseet jätettiin aseellisten kirkkoon</Line>
        <Line>astuessa) päätyseinässä on käytäwä,</Line>
        <Line>joka wie owen yläpuolella olewalle au-</Line>
        <Line>kolle. Toisinaan nämät tällaiset käy-</Line>
        <Line>täwät wiewät jostain kirkonsisäpuolisesta</Line>
        <Line>nurkasta kirkon seiniin tehtyihin auk-</Line>
        <Line>koihin. Nämät käytäwät aukkoineen teh-</Line>
        <Line>tiin arwattawasti paawinaikuisten pap-</Line>
        <Line>pien kirkollisia temppuja warten. Päl-</Line>
        <Line>käneen, melkein kamalassa, wanhassa</Line>
        <Line>kirkossa ei ollut enää nähtäwänä muuta</Line>
        <Line>kirkollista tarwekalua, kuin wanha pui-</Line>
        <Line>nen kasteenmalja. Helsinkiin on lähe-</Line>
        <Line>tetty 8 pyhäin-kuwaa y. m. Uudessa</Line>
        <Line>kirkossa säilytetään kahden sadan wuo-</Line>
        <Line>tuisia waakunoita y. m. Uusi kirkko</Line>
        <Line>Pälkäneellä rakennettiin ww. 1836—39</Line>
        <Line>arkitehdin Engel'in antaman piirustuk-</Line>
        <Line>sen mukaan.</Line>
      </Paragraph>

        <Line>A. D. H.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Tuo on kummallinen kansa tuo Rans-</Line>
        <Line>kan kansa. Sen suuri historioitsija La-</Line>
        <Line>martine on sanonut jossakussa teokses-</Line>
        <Line>saan: „Jos Jumala tahtoo, että uusi</Line>
        <Line>ajatus käypi halki mailman, niin Hän</Line>
        <Line>sen ajatuksen synnyttää Ranskalaisen rin-</Line>
        <Line>nassa". Niinpä niin! Tämän histo-</Line>
        <Line>rioitsijansa Ranskalaisille antamaa kii-</Line>
        <Line>tosta eiwät nykyiset Ranskalaiset tahdo</Line>
        <Line>ottaa muistaaksensa, olla maailman ete-</Line>
        <Line>wimpänä kansana, eikä myöskään seu-</Line>
        <Line>rataksensa. Jos joitakuita onnenkohte-</Line>
        <Line>loita on jotakuta kansaa tawannut ja ta-</Line>
        <Line>woittanut, on se Ranskan kansaa. Jo-</Line>
        <Line>kaisella tämän lehden lukijalla lienee</Line>
        <Line>tuoreessa muistissa, mitenkä Preussiläi-</Line>
        <Line>set, Saksalaiset woitoisasti otteliwat</Line>
        <Line>Ranskan kansan kanssa. Silloin hädän</Line>
        <Line>hetkenä nousi eräs jalo mies, toisten</Line>
        <Line>milt'ei kaikki toiweet isänmaan pelastuk-</Line>
        <Line>sesta heitettyä, esiin, oudonmoisella in-</Line>
        <Line>nostuksellaan innostuttaen koko kansaansa.</Line>
        <Line>Jäljestäpäin on tätä miestä kunnioitettu</Line>
        <Line>ja on hän wiime aikoina ollut Ranskan</Line>
        <Line>meidän waltiopäiwihin werrattawien</Line>
        <Line>Ranskan maalla pidettyjen waltiopäi-</Line>
        <Line>wäin puheenjohtajana. Puheessa ole-</Line>
        <Line>wan miehen nimi on Gambetta. Kai-</Line>
        <Line>ken kansan silmät luottiwat hänehen ja</Line>
        <Line>luopuen maltiopäiwä-toimistansa täytyi</Line>
        <Line>hänen muutama kuukausi sitte ottaa Rans-</Line>
        <Line>kan waltion ohjat käsiinsä. Nytkö Rans-</Line>
        <Line>kalaiset tyytyiwät kun saiwat heiltä yksin-</Line>
        <Line>omaisesti kutsutun „Suuren kansalaisensa"</Line>
        <Line>ministöristönsä päälliköksi? Wielä kai!</Line>
        <Line>Ranskan kansa on sellainen kansa, ett'-</Line>
        <Line>eiwät sen parhaimmatkaan miehet kelpaa</Line>
        <Line>sitä ohjaamaan. Gambetta ja hänen</Line>
        <Line>ministöristönsä woidaan pitää kuoleman</Line>
        <Line>tuomion saaneina, mutta löytyykö aino-</Line>
        <Line>atakaan miestä Ranskan kansassa, joka</Line>
        <Line>woisi waltion ohjia, hänen ne jätetty-</Line>
        <Line>änsä, ottaa wastaan? Gambetta on epäi-</Line>
        <Line>lemättä Ranskan kansan etewin mies</Line>
        <Line>ja jospa Ranskalaiset eiwät tahdo hänen</Line>
        <Line>toimittamaan hallitukseensa tyytyä —</Line>
        <Line>niin olkoot hallitusta paitsi. Ikäwää</Line>
        <Line>on kuulla ja lukea kuinka puolueriitaiset</Line>
        <Line>lehdet tältä mieheltä tahtowat riistää</Line>
        <Line>sen kunnian, jonka hän on ansainnut.</Line>
        <Line>Tähän lehteen ei suoda sijaa sellaisille</Line>
        <Line>parjaamisille, waan on sydämellinen toi-</Line>
        <Line>wotuksemme olewa: Eläköön Lamartine'n</Line>
        <Line>kansan jaloin poika ja onnistukoot hä-</Line>
        <Line>nen tehtämänsä!</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Ranskan asia Tunesia’ssa *) sanotaan</Line>
        <Line>olewan parantumista päin.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Portugal'issa on seurattu Ranskan</Line>
        <Line>kansan tapoja. Entinen Herra Fonte-</Line>
        <Line>sia'n johdattama ministeristö on nimit-</Line>
        <Line>täin saatu kumotuksi eikä hänen sijaansa</Line>
        <Line>kuulu saatawan sopiwaa miestä. Herra</Line>
        <Line>Pimentel, nykyjään Parisissa asuwa, on</Line>
        <Line>kutsuttu uuden kabinetin johtajaksi. Saa-</Line>
        <Line>daanpas nähdä, josko hän saa tuon pienen</Line>
        <Line>kuningaskunnan asiat hywälle kannalle.</Line>
        <Line>Sen tulewaisuus on osoittawa.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>uskaltaa vielä edeskinpäin toivoa voi-</Line>
        <Line>vansa vyöttää kupeensa ja lähteä mat-</Line>
        <Line>kalle Suomen sakeille saloille; toivoopa</Line>
        <Line>vielä sieltäkin löytävänsä tuommoisia</Line>
        <Line>ikihonkia ja tervaskantoja, joista ka-</Line>
        <Line>raistu ja „sliipattu" teränsä voisi tuot-</Line>
        <Line>taa sytykettä, jos ei summia suurem-</Line>
        <Line>pia niin ainakin tuluksien tarpeiksi.</Line>
        <Line>Niin on hommat hyörimässä, kohta</Line>
        <Line>tuumatkin tukussa. — Alla päin, pa-</Line>
        <Line>hoilla mielin tunnustaa Pilkkakirveenne</Line>
        <Line>entisen hienon pelkonsa, jonka kah-</Line>
        <Line>leissa tuo hoettu „Marraskuun 15</Line>
        <Line>päivä" häntä on pidellyt. Sepä se on-</Line>
        <Line>kin ollut syynä, ettei Pilkkakirveenne</Line>
        <Line>ole monastikaan uskaltanut lähteä mök-</Line>
        <Line>kinsä kynnystä loitommalle henkisellä</Line>
        <Line>alalla, vaan on täytynyt „tuhassa" is-</Line>
        <Line>tuen vajavaisuuksiaan muistella. Nyt</Line>
        <Line>on kumminkin aika jo toinen: on päästy</Line>
        <Line>tuosta pälkähästä ja nythän jo heti</Line>
        <Line>eletään uuden annakan avulla; eikäpä</Line>
        <Line>tuo uusi annakka olekkan niin pahoilla</Line>
        <Line>ennemerkeillä täytetty, kuin se, joka</Line>
        <Line>kohta riekaleina on. Senpätähden lu-</Line>
        <Line>paa Pilkkakirveenne esiytyä tulevana</Line>
        <Line>vuonna taas entistä „imelämmällä tuu-</Line>
        <Line>lella", jos kohtakin koolla entisellä,</Line>
        <Line>varoen kumminkin, etteivät lukijansa</Line>
        <Line>liiasta naurusta kuoliaiksi pakahtuisi.</Line>
        <Line>Kuvista pitää Pilkkakirveen „panoraa-</Line>
        <Line>maosasto" huolta kykynsä mukaan, yk-</Line>
        <Line>sin kukkaroltansakaan lupaa kysymättä.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Vieläpä lupaa hätä-tiloissa kysyä</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Kuinka tarkkaan kuuntelinkin, en sa-</Line>

        <Line>Olihan wainajan aina ollut tapana kir-</Line>

        <Line>mahtawuudella korwataksensa sitä, mikä</Line>

        <Line>kelwollista; ja olikin ukolla tässä suh-</Line>
        <Line>teessa ollut paljon korwattawaa — niin</Line>
        <Line>ainakin ilweiliwät jotkut wiisastelewat</Line>
        <Line>seurakuntalaiset. — Waan maltappas!</Line>
        <Line>Mikä kauhea jyske oli tuo, joka wast'i-</Line>
        <Line>kään kuului kirkosta, saaden kaikki sen</Line>
        <Line>akkunat tärisemään? Wereni oli jääksi</Line>
        <Line>jäähtyä — niin kowin säikähdyin. Waan</Line>
        <Line>johan tuo kamala kolina taukosi kuulu-</Line>
        <Line>masta. — Mitäpäs maar'! Kotwasen ku-</Line>
        <Line>luttua, uutta jyskyntää, kirkon kaarrok-</Line>
        <Line>set uudestaan kajahtamaan, sen akkunat</Line>
        <Line>tärähtelemään! — Mutta tällä kertaa</Line>
        <Line>kajasi tuo jyske raskaiden askelten kai-</Line>
        <Line>kuna. Jättiläisetkö siellä wiettiwät har-</Line>
        <Line>tauttansa tänä yönä? Kenenkä muun</Line>
        <Line>kuin jättiläisen askeleet woisiwat nostaa</Line>
        <Line>niin kowaa pauhinaa, kuin tuon olen-</Line>
        <Line>non, jonka askeleita kuulollani saatoin</Line>
        <Line>seurata kun se alttarin tyköä asteli kir-</Line>
        <Line>kon owea kohti. Jo oli se saapunut</Line>
        <Line>kirkon owelle saakka; minä kuulin kuinka</Line>
        <Line>owi rätisten sarannoillansa aukeni ja</Line>
        <Line>kuinka se sitten hirmuisella jyskinällä</Line>

ومع غيره فلو كان عملك مع جورج وحده لما كان لنا وانظمة لمدحك لان اهالك بالعمل
ولكن لما كان يقول جورج للمجروح الذين عندنا ما فقد طلب معونه من موسَى فرحات
ورده خاطيا فناك ململ ان اعمالك عن خنود شهاده وحسب فكان راسَي يقطع البحر
من ذيابون ارتفاعه بك فابدّ ان من يخلف لا يموت فصاحب الميراث فرح لم ينقول
بعَا يخفض ولد فرحات وولده موسَى (فهذا النبيل من عربي ذاكر الاسَد)
يحف للشاب الاقتخار بك لانك الحداثة شبك فعلت ملا بقلا الشبوخ من الخير
لذهما عاملنا اولاد الغير احسَن لما يعامل الغير اولادهم ذاهم. وبلا شك الله يبروقكم
ماء بار و اجر لا يصبع اقول هذا باختصار لانه من تاريخ ١٢ الجاري لان عملي
مفقود واراد القربة وضدهم نفروق ذرافان بفرع البيت ويخبلى منهم حني
انه بعون التلثه عشريونا اضرمنا لذه النوم
ولكن ارمعة المرحوم سَعيد وضحوه ودموتها التي لا تقطع اهلها الدمتى ان انرك
الجمهور واحدركم نحرجها وهذا التحرير ومن الجدالك على تحريرها غنابية وانا اقولكم
اذا كان صغير فول جورج او غير صغير فلوج الله ارجوك ان يضيف ما من
جدية الى ما ترك الخديبة وندلعب بذاتك اذا امكن للتلكلك الجبان ونصحى

ридското езеро. Охридското езеро е яйцевидно, продълговато и отъ

гатъ току изъ водитѣ на езерото; западнитѣ ридини наблизу до
езерото не сѫ по високи отъ обикновенъ брѣгъ, когато источнитѣ
заловени съ планински възвишенности сѫ доста високи. Тѣзи двѣ-
тѣ противоположни възвишенности или ридове около езерото про-
дължаватъ своята успоредна посока и на сѣверъ отъ езерото и об-
разувания тука отъ тѣхъ ридъ е межда на Охридското по малко
и Стружското по-голѣмо полета, раздѣлявани отъ единъ обособенъ
планински връхъ, наричанъ Вишовска и частно Гѫбавска и Чекош-
чика планина. Въ сѣверо-источния кѫть на езерото е отсоченъ мал-
ко единъ по-възвишенъ ридъ, който изгледва като полукрѫгъ, про-
стрѣнъ на длъжъ около единъ часъ; този полукрѫгъ. ошира о е-

високъ до 300 нозѣ надъ езерото, а источний е нѣщо по низъкъ.
На този полукрѫгъ, и по отлозитѣ на реченнитѣ върховци, отъ ед-

      </Heading>

        <Line>দিবাস্বপ্নশ্চ তৃটশূল হিক্কা জীর্ণাতিসারিণাং।।</Line>

  <Page>
    <Header>
      <Heading>
        <Line>কৃষিকার্য্যের মত।</Line>
      </Heading>
      <PageNumber>৪৫</PageNumber>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>অতএব কৃষিকর্ম্মের উৎকর্ষ সাধন করিতে হইলে</Line>
        <Line>শেষোক্ত উপায়ই অগ্রে অবলম্বন করা বিধেয়।</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>এস্থলে এরূপ আশঙ্কা। হইতে পারে, যে যদিও</Line>
        <Line>উক্তরূপ কার্য্য করিলে শীঘ্র কৃষি কার্যের উন্নতি হ</Line>
        <Line>ইবে বটে, কিন্তু ইচ্ছ। পূর্ব্বক কোন্ ভদ্র বংশীয় কৃত</Line>
        <Line>বিদা যুবক, তাদৃশ কৰ্ম্মে প্রবৃত্ত হইবে? বাস্ত-</Line>
        <Line>বিক, সে আশঙ্ক। নিতান্ত অমূলক সন্দেহ নাই।</Line>
        <Line>যে হেতু, এবিষয়ে কৃতবিদ্য যুবকদিগের অনভিমত</Line>
        <Line>হইবার সম্ভাবনা দেখা যাইতেছে না। কাহারো</Line>
        <Line>নিকট স্বাধীনতা বিক্রয় করতঃ বেতনভুকু হইয়া,</Line>
        <Line>চাকুরিতে নিযুক্ত হওয়া, আর কৃষি কার্য করিয়া সুখ</Line>
        <Line>সচ্ছন্দতায় সংসার যাত্রানিব্বাহ করা, এই উভয়ের</Line>
        <Line>মধ্যে, কি ইতরবিশেষ আছে, তাহা কৃতবিদ্য যুব।</Line>
        <Line>দল উত্তমরূপে অবগত আছেন। তাঁহারা এখন বু-</Line>
        <Line>ঝিতে পারিয়াছেন, যে স্বাধীনতা কি অমূল্যরত্ন</Line>
        <Line>এবং স্বাধীনতার গুণ কি। স্বাধীনতা সকল সুখের</Line>
        <Line>আকর। যাহার স্বাধীনতা নাই সে চিরদুঃখী। স্বা-</Line>
        <Line>ধীনতা না থাকিলে লোক নিতান্ত ভীক হয়; ভীৰু</Line>
        <Line>অন্তঃকরণ পাপের আবাস ভূমি। ভীক অন্তঃকরণে</Line>
        <Line>কদাপি ধর্ম প্রবৃত্তির জীবন্তভাব থাকে না। পরাধীন</Line>
      </Paragraph>
    </Body>
  </Page>
</HistoricalDocument>

<HistoricalDocument xmlns="http://example.com/historicaldocument">
  <Metadata>
    <Language>English</Language>
    <WritingDirection>ltr</WritingDirection>
    <PhysicalDescription>Single page from a printed newspaper.</PhysicalDescription>
    <Description>Page 581 of The Examiner, dated 1845, featuring articles on exploration, native customs, theatrical reviews, and foreign news.</Description>
    <Script>Latin</Script>
  </Metadata>
  <Page>
    <Header>
      <Heading type="other">
        <Line>1845.]</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>THE EXAMINER.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <PageNumber>581</PageNumber>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>eat the dry and withered grass around us. We now lay</Line>
        <Line>down to rest ourselves, and the boy soon fell asleep ; I was</Line>
        <Line>however feverish and restless, and could not close my eyes.</Line>
        <Line>In an hour and a half I arose, got up the horses and saddled</Line>
        <Line>them, and then, awaking my companion, we again pushed</Line>
        <Line>on by moonlight. At ten miles we crossed a well‐beaten</Line>
        <Line>native pathway, plainly discernible even then, and this we</Line>
        <Line>followed down towards the cliﬀs, fully hoping it would lead</Line>
        <Line>to water. Our hopes, however, had been excited but to</Line>
        <Line>render our disappointment the greater, for upon tracing it</Line>
        <Line>onwards we found it terminate abruptly at a large circular</Line>
        <Line>hole of limestone rock, which would retain a considerable</Line>
        <Line>quantity of water after rains, but was now without a single</Line>
        <Line>drop. Gloomily turning away we again pushed on for</Line>
        <Line>eight miles further, and at three in the morning of the 10th</Line>
        <Line>were compelled to halt from downright exhaustion and</Line>
        <Line>fatigue. The horses and sheep were knocked up. The</Line>
        <Line>poor boy was so tired and sleepy that he could scarcely sit</Line>
        <Line>upon his horse, and I found myself actually dosing as I</Line>
        <Line>walked : mechanically my legs kept moving forwards, but</Line>
        <Line>my eyes were every now and then closed in forgetfulness of</Line>
        <Line>all around me, until I was suddenly thrown down by get‑</Line>
        <Line>ting entangled amongst the scrub, or aroused by a severe</Line>
        <Line>blow across the face from the recoil of a bough after the</Line>
        <Line>passage of the boy's horse. I now judged we had come</Line>
        <Line>about ninety‐three miles from Yeerkum‐ban‐kauwe, and</Line>
        <Line>hoped that we could not be very far from water. Having</Line>
        <Line>tied up the horses for an hour or two, and without making</Line>
        <Line>a ﬁre, or even unrolling our cloaks to cover us, we stretched</Line>
        <Line>ourselves on the ground, and were in a few moments fast</Line>
        <Line>asleep.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" March 10.—At ﬁve we were again on our route, every</Line>
        <Line>moment expecting to see a break in the line of cliﬀs along</Line>
        <Line>which we had now travelled so far. Alas ! they still con‑</Line>
        <Line>tinued stretching as far as the eye could see to the west‑</Line>
        <Line>ward, and as fast as we arrived at one point which had</Line>
        <Line>bounded our vision ( and beyond which we hoped a change</Line>
        <Line>might occur), it was but to be met with the view of another</Line>
        <Line>beyond. Distressing and fatal as the continuance of these</Line>
        <Line>cliﬀs might prove to us, there was a grandeur and sub‑</Line>
        <Line>limity in their appearance that was most imposing, and</Line>
        <Line>which struck me with admiration. Stretching out before</Line>
        <Line>us in lofty unbroken outline, they presented the singular</Line>
        <Line>and romantic appearance of massy battlements of masonry,</Line>
        <Line>supported by huge buttresses, and glittering in the morn‑</Line>
        <Line>ing sun which had now risen upon them, and made the</Line>
        <Line>scene beautiful even amidst the dangers and anxieties of</Line>
        <Line>our situation."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>In a direct line of upwards of 800 miles thus</Line>
        <Line>gone over by Mr Eyre, there does not seem to</Line>
        <Line>have been a watercourse, or a hollow of any kind,</Line>
        <Line>crossed ; and not a drop of fresh water accessible</Line>
        <Line>on the surface. It could only be obtained by dig‑</Line>
        <Line>ging close to the sea‐shore, or the sand‐hills of the</Line>
        <Line>coast ; and even by that means was often not pro‑</Line>
        <Line>curable for distances of 160 miles together. The</Line>
        <Line>dreary waste is described by Mr Eyre as an almost</Line>
        <Line>uniform table land of fossil formation, with an ele‑</Line>
        <Line>vation of from three to ﬁve hundred feet ; covered</Line>
        <Line>for the most part by dense impenetrable scrubs,</Line>
        <Line>and only varied on its surface by occasional sandy</Line>
        <Line>or rocky undulations. The dangers and suﬀerings</Line>
        <Line>of travel in such a region may be conceived ; as</Line>
        <Line>well as its generally uninteresting character. But</Line>
        <Line>every now and then a startling little trait occurs</Line>
        <Line>which gives the living touch of reality to the scene ;</Line>
        <Line>and again carries the reader forward, watchful and</Line>
        <Line>anxious for the traveller. In the following for</Line>
        <Line>instance.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" . . . I occupied myself in writing and charting during</Line>
        <Line>the day, and at night amused myself in taking stellar obser‑</Line>
        <Line>vations for latitude. I had already taken the altitude of Vega,</Line>
        <Line>and deduced the latitude to be 32 deg. 3 min. 23 sec. S. ;</Line>
        <Line>leaving my artiﬁcial horizon on the ground outside whilst I</Line>
        <Line>remained in the tent waiting until Altair came to the meri‑</Line>
        <Line>dian, I then took my sextant and went out to observe this</Line>
        <Line>star also ; but upon putting down my hand to take hold of</Line>
        <Line>the horizon‐glass in order to wipe the dew oﬀ, my ﬁngers</Line>
        <Line>went into the quicksilver—the horizon‐glass was gone, and</Line>
        <Line>also the piece of canvas I had put on the ground to lie down</Line>
        <Line>upon whilst observing so low an altitude as that of Vega.</Line>
        <Line>Searching a little more, I missed a spade, a parcel of horse‑</Line>
        <Line>shoes, an axe, a tin dish, some ropes, a grubbing‐hoe, and</Line>
        <Line>several smaller things which had been left outside the tent,</Line>
        <Line>as not being likely to take any injury from the damp. It</Line>
        <Line>was evident I was surrounded by natives, who had stolen</Line>
        <Line>all these things during the short time I had been in my tent,</Line>
        <Line>certainly not exceeding half an hour. The night was very</Line>
        <Line>windy, and I had heard nothing ; besides, I was encamped</Line>
        <Line>in the midst of a very dense brush of large wide‐spreading</Line>
        <Line>tea‐trees and other bushes, any of which would aﬀord a</Line>
        <Line>screen for a considerable number of natives. In daylight it</Line>
        <Line>was impossible to see many yards in distance, and nothing</Line>
        <Line>could be discerned at night. . . . As soon as I</Line>
        <Line>missed my horizon‐glass, and entertained the suspicion</Line>
        <Line>of natives being about. I hurried into the tent, and</Line>
        <Line>lighting a large blue light, run with it rapidly through</Line>
        <Line>the bushes around me. The eﬀect of this was very beauti‑</Line>
        <Line>ful amidst the darkness and gloom of the woods, and for a</Line>
        <Line>great distance in every direction objects could be seen as</Line>
        <Line>well as by day : the natives, however, were gone ; and I</Line>
        <Line>could only console myself by ﬁring a couple of balls after</Line>
        <Line>them through the underwood, to warn them of the danger</Line>
        <Line>of intruding upon me again. I then put everything which</Line>
        <Line>had been left outside into the tent, and kept watch for an</Line>
        <Line>hour or two; but my visitors came no more. . . . Rising</Line>
        <Line>very early, I set to work with an axe to clear away the</Line>
        <Line>bushes from around my tent. I now discovered that the</Line>
        <Line>natives had been concealed behind a large tea‐tree not</Line>
        <Line>twenty yards from the tent : there were numerous foot‑</Line>
        <Line>marks there, and the remains of ﬁre‐sticks which they had</Line>
        <Line>brought with them, for a native rarely moves at night with‑</Line>
        <Line>out ﬁre."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mr Eyre seems to have no hope, in spite of</Line>
        <Line>Capt. Sturt's cheering dispatches, that any inland</Line>
        <Line>sea will ever be ultimately discovered behind this</Line>
        <Line>vast unpromising table land. Can it be, he asks,</Line>
        <Line>that the whole is one immense interminable desert,</Line>
        <Line>" or an alternation of deserts and shallow lakes ?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Incidental to the narrative of the expeditions</Line>
        <Line>are many illustrations of native character : but Mr</Line>
        <Line>Eyre, as we before said, has collected all his many</Line>
        <Line>years' experiences on this head into a separate</Line>
        <Line>treatise or dissertation at the close of his work.</Line>
        <Line>The reader interested in the subject will ﬁnd his</Line>
        <Line>information curious and ample. The matters</Line>
        <Line>treated of embrace not only the physical and moral</Line>
        <Line>state of the aborigines ; their habits of life, rude</Line>
        <Line>government, and social relations ; their language</Line>
        <Line>and dialects ; but also very interesting notices of</Line>
        <Line>the eﬀects of their contact with Europeans, and</Line>
        <Line>some valuable suggestions for an improvement in</Line>
        <Line>the system generally adopted towards them.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Our extracts are limited by our space : but to</Line>
        <Line>even readers familiar with Captain Grey's excellent</Line>
        <Line>dissertations, much of Mr Eyre's information will</Line>
        <Line>be new and original.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>HUSBAND AND WIFE.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" Wives are considered the absolute property of the hus‑</Line>
        <Line>band, and can be given away, or exchanged, or lent, ac‑</Line>
        <Line>cording to his caprice. A husband is denominated in the</Line>
        <Line>Adelaide dialect, Yongarra, Martanya (the owner or pro‑</Line>
        <Line>prietor of a wife). Female children are betrothed usually</Line>
        <Line>from early infancy, and such arrangements are usually ad‑</Line>
        <Line>hered to ; still in many cases circumstances occur frequently</Line>
        <Line>to cause an alteration ; but if not, the girls generally go to</Line>
        <Line>live with their husbands about the age of twelve, and some‑</Line>
        <Line>times even before that. Relatives nearer than cousins are</Line>
        <Line>not allowed to marry, and this alliance does not generally</Line>
        <Line>take place Female orphans belong to the nearest male re‑</Line>
        <Line>lative, as also does a widow, instead of to the nearest male</Line>
        <Line>relative of the husband, as was found to be the case in</Line>
        <Line>Western Australia by Captain Grey. Two or three months</Line>
        <Line>generally elapse before the widow goes to another hus‑</Line>
        <Line>band ; but if the wife dies, the man takes another as soon</Line>
        <Line>as he can get one. If a woman, having young children,</Line>
        <Line>join another tribe, the children go with her ; but I am not</Line>
        <Line>aware whether they would remain permanently attached to</Line>
        <Line>that tribe or not. Brothers often barter their sisters for</Line>
        <Line>wives for themselves, but it can only be done with the</Line>
        <Line>parents' consent, or after their death. If a wife be stolen,</Line>
        <Line>war is always continued until she is given up, or another</Line>
        <Line>female in her place.</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" There is no ceremony connected with the undertaking</Line>
        <Line>of marriage. In those cases where I have witnessed the</Line>
        <Line>giving away of a wife, the woman was simply ordered by</Line>
        <Line>the nearest male relative in whose disposal she was, to take</Line>
        <Line>up her ' rocko,' the bag in which a female carries the eﬀects</Line>
        <Line>of her husband, and go to the man's camp to whom she had</Line>
        <Line>been given. Marriage is not looked upon as any pledge of</Line>
        <Line>chastity, indeed no such virtue is recognised. But little</Line>
        <Line>real aﬀection consequently exists between husbands and</Line>
        <Line>wives, and young men value a wife principally for her ser‑</Line>
        <Line>vices as a slave ; in fact, when asked why they are anxious</Line>
        <Line>to obtain wives, their usual reply is, that they may get</Line>
        <Line>wood, water, and food for them, and carry whatever pro‑</Line>
        <Line>perty they possess."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>NATIVE MODESTY.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" Innate propriety of behaviour is also frequently exhi‑</Line>
        <Line>bited by the Aborigines in their natural state, in the modest</Line>
        <Line>unasuming manner in which they take their positions to</Line>
        <Line>observe what is going on, and in a total absence of any‑</Line>
        <Line>thing that is rude or oﬀensive. It is true that the reverse</Line>
        <Line>of this is also often to be met with ; but I think it will</Line>
        <Line>usually be found that it is among natives who have before</Line>
        <Line>been in contact with Europeans, or where familiarities have</Line>
        <Line>been used with them ﬁrst, or an injudicious system of treat‑</Line>
        <Line>ment has been adopted towards them.</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" Delicacy of feeling is not often laid to the charge of the</Line>
        <Line>Aborigines, and yet I was witness to a singular instance of</Line>
        <Line>it at King George's Sound. I was looking one evening at</Line>
        <Line>the natives dancing, and who were, as they always are on</Line>
        <Line>these occasions, in a state of complete nudity. In the</Line>
        <Line>midst of the performance, one of the natives standing by as</Line>
        <Line>a spectator, mentioned that a white woman was passing up</Line>
        <Line>the road ; and although this was some little distance away,</Line>
        <Line>and the night was tolerably dark, they all with one accord</Line>
        <Line>crossed over to the bushes where their cloaks were, put</Line>
        <Line>them on, and resumed their amusement."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Some representations of native ornaments, wea‑</Line>
        <Line>pons, and implements and works of industry, in</Line>
        <Line>this part of the book, are useful to the text.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>THE THEATRICAL EXAMINER.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>HAYMARKET.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The False Mr Pope is a retired Hammersmith</Line>
        <Line>tradesman of about ﬁve feet four, with a Ramilie</Line>
        <Line>wig and tail more than half as big as himself,</Line>
        <Line>square‐cut buckram skirts, long ﬂapped white</Line>
        <Line>waistcoat, and minute three‐cornered hat, who is</Line>
        <Line>passed oﬀ by a wag of a player upon a party of</Line>
        <Line>petticoat admirers of Pope, for the celebrated au‑</Line>
        <Line>thor of the Dunciad. To fancy Mr Buckstone in</Line>
        <Line>this predicament, is to have a very clear notion of</Line>
        <Line>Mr Peake's amusing farce.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>It is nicely presented ; with abundance of pe‑</Line>
        <Line>ruke for the gentlemen, and of hoods, clustering</Line>
        <Line>curls, cardinals, and little china, for the ladies ; and</Line>
        <Line>it perpetrates a vast many abominable jokes, which</Line>
        <Line>nobody but the actors and actresses can possibly</Line>
        <Line>be expected to laugh at. But this is the " moral."</Line>
        <Line>The ladies are in such a state of frantic foregone</Line>
        <Line>admiration of Mr Pope, that the more audacious</Line>
        <Line>the ﬂights of Mr Buckstone the wittier they are</Line>
        <Line>taken to be ; and though this is rather a danger‑</Line>
        <Line>ous experiment for a farce, the audience help it</Line>
        <Line>out with their good‐nature.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Indeed it would take a troublesome amount of</Line>
        <Line>the other quality to withstand Mr Buckstone's</Line>
        <Line>practical points of drollery. When he takes oﬀ</Line>
        <Line>his wig in a sudden heat, for example, and exposes</Line>
        <Line>his small bald head. Swift's mouse under a canopy</Line>
        <Line>of state is nothing to it. When he eﬀects a series</Line>
        <Line>of practical Rapes of the Lock, too, he uses the</Line>
        <Line>scissors like a true poet. And when he passes</Line>
        <Line>from doing to suﬀering, tastes the griefs as well as</Line>
        <Line>glories of fame, and is well thrashed by Mr Curll's</Line>
        <Line>chairman as he leaves the player's house,—the act</Line>
        <Line>closed with a roar. There should have been no</Line>
        <Line>second. There is nothing but stale repetition in</Line>
        <Line>the second act. The ladies retort with a practical</Line>
        <Line>joke of their own, which is much more remarkable</Line>
        <Line>for its dullness than for any more lady‐like quality.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>LYCEUM.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>An excellent new farce was played here on Mon‑</Line>
        <Line>day night ; better than any piece of its class which</Line>
        <Line>we have seen for many a day. It has nicety of</Line>
        <Line>character, and a good broad humour. You laugh,</Line>
        <Line>and have no need to be ashamed of your mirth.</Line>
        <Line>There is neither caricature nor coarseness. We</Line>
        <Line>cannot stay to tell the plot (which is a plot, and</Line>
        <Line>not told without some pains), but must brieﬂy</Line>
        <Line>counsel the playgoer to see Peter Jenkins. Mr</Line>
        <Line>and Mrs Keeley, Mr Wigan and Mr Meadows,</Line>
        <Line>complete an admirable cast. Mr Keeley is not</Line>
        <Line>only an honest truth‐telling fellow forced to tell</Line>
        <Line>lies for a friend ; but a conﬁrmed little bachelor,</Line>
        <Line>caught, willy‐nilly, in the snares of matrimony.</Line>
        <Line>His dilemmas are intense, and he does justice to</Line>
        <Line>them.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>FOREIGN NEWS.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>FRANCE.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>DEATH OF M. ROYER COLLARD.—This illustrious</Line>
        <Line>citizen died on the 4th inst., at his estate at Chateauvieux,</Line>
        <Line>near Saint‐Aignan, in the 82nd year of his age. M.</Line>
        <Line>Royer Collard had been President of the Chamber of De‑</Line>
        <Line>puties, Member of the French Academy, and Professor of</Line>
        <Line>Philosophy at the College of France.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>THE SLAVE TRADE CONVENTION.—" The vessels in‑</Line>
        <Line>tended to act against the slave trade are not," says the</Line>
        <Line>' Constitutionnel,' " yet ready to proceed to the coasts of</Line>
        <Line>Africa. They are not to set out for six weeks or two</Line>
        <Line>months. Meanwhile communications are exchanged with</Line>
        <Line>England every day on the subject of the mission which</Line>
        <Line>the two navies are to fulﬁl together. Recently the Ad‑</Line>
        <Line>miralty has drawn up regulations for day and night sig‑</Line>
        <Line>nals, which the English and French cruisers are to make</Line>
        <Line>use of, in order to mutually recognise each other. It ap‑</Line>
        <Line>pears that we have approved of all the dispositions of</Line>
        <Line>these regulations. It is divided into two parts ; the ﬁrst</Line>
        <Line>concerning sailing vessels, and the other steamers. The</Line>
        <Line>English navy has been long occupied for its own use with</Line>
        <Line>a regulation of this kind for steamers, collisions of which</Line>
        <Line>are both frequent and dangerous. In France, nothing</Line>
        <Line>has been done in that respect."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>RUMOURED RETIREMENT OF MARSHAL SOULT.—A</Line>

down to rest ourselves, and the boy soon fell asleep; I was

In an hour and a half I arose, got up the horses and saddled
them, and then, awaking my companion, we again pushed

native pathway, plainly discernible even then, and this we
followed down towards the cliffs, fully hoping it would lead

render our disappointment the greater, for upon tracing it
onwards we found it terminate at a large circular
hole of limestone rock, which would retain a considerable
quantity of water after rains, but was now without a single
drop. Gloomily turning away we again pushed on for
eight miles further, and at three in the morning of the 10th
were compelled to halt from downright exhaustion and
fatigue. The horses and sheep were knocked up. The
poor boy was so tired and sleepy that he could scarcely sit
upon his horse, and I found myself actually dosing as I
walked: mechanically my legs kept moving forwards, but
my eyes were every now and then closed in forgetfulness of
all around me, until I was suddenly thrown down by get-
ting entangled amongst the scrub, or aroused by a severe
blow across the face from the recoil of a bough after the
passage of the boy's horse. I now judged we had come
about ninety-three miles from Yeerkum-ban-kauwe, and
hoped that we could not be very far from water. Having
tied up the horses for an hour or two, and without making
a fire, or even unrolling our cloaks to cover us, we stretched
ourselves on the ground, and were in a few moments fast
asleep.
"March 10.—At five we were again on our route, every
moment expecting to see a break in the line of cliffs along
which we had now travelled so far. Alas! they still con-
tinued stretching as far as the eye could see to the west-
ward, and as fast as we arrived at one point which had
bounded our vision (and beyond which we hoped a change
might occur), it was but to be met with the view of another
beyond. Distressing and fatal as the continuance of these
cliffs might prove to us, there was a grandeur and sub-
limity in their appearance that was most imposing, and
which struck me with admiration. Stretching out before
us in lofty unbroken outline, they presented the singular
and romantic appearance of massy battlements of masonry,
supported by huge buttresses, and glittering in the morn-
ing sun which had now risen upon them, and made the
scene beautiful even amidst the dangers and anxieties of
our situation."
In a direct line of upwards of 800 miles thus
gone over by Mr Eyre, there does not seem to
have been a watercourse, or a hollow of any kind,
crossed; and not a drop of fresh water accessible
on the surface. It could only be obtained by dig-
ging close to the sea-shore, or the sand-hills of the
coast; and even by that means was often not pro-
curable for distances of 160 miles together. The
dreary waste is described by Mr Eyre as an almost
uniform table land of fossil formation, with an ele-
vation of from three to five hundred feet; covered
for the most part by dense impenetrable scrubs,
and only varied on its surface by occasional sandy
or rocky undulations. The dangers and sufferings
of travel in such a region may be conceived; as
well as its generally uninteresting character. But
every now and then a startling little trait occurs
which gives the living touch of reality to the scene;
and again carries the reader forward, watchful and
anxious for the traveller. In the following for
instance.
" . . I occupied myself in writing and charting during
the day, and at night amused myself in taking stellar obser-
vations for latitude. I had already taken the altitude of Vega,
and deduced the latitude to be 32 deg. 3 min. 23 sec. S.;
leaving my artificial horizon on the ground outside whilst I
remained in the tent waiting until Altair came to the meri-
dian. I then took my sextant and went out to observe this
star also; but upon putting down my hand to take hold of
the horizon-glass in order to wipe the dew off, my fingers
went into the quicksilver—the horizon-glass was gone, and
also the piece of canvas I had put on the ground to lie down
upon whilst observing so low an altitude as that of Vega.
Searching a little more, I missed a spade, a parcel of horse-
shoes, an axe, a tin dish, some ropes, a grubbing-hoe, and
several smaller things which had been left outside the tent,
as not being likely to take any injury from the damp. It
was evident I was surrounded by natives, who had stolen
all these things during the short time I had been in my tent,
certainly not exceeding half an hour. The night was very
windy, and I had heard nothing; besides, I was encamped
in the midst of a very dense brush of large wide-spreading
tea-trees and other bushes, any of which would afford a
screen for a considerable number of natives. In daylight it
was impossible to see many yards in distance, and nothing
could be discerned at night. . . As soon as I
missed my horizon-glass, and entertained the suspicion
of natives being about, I hurried into the tent, and
lighting a large blue light, run with it rapidly through
the bushes around me. The effect of this was very beauti-
ful amidst the darkness and gloom of the woods, and for a
great distance in every direction objects could be seen as
well as by day: the natives, however, were gone; and I
could only console myself by firing a couple of balls after
them through the underwood, to warn them of the danger
of intruding upon me again. I then put everything which
had been left outside into the tent, and kept watch for an
hour or two; but my visitors came no more. . . Rising
very early, I set to work with an axe to clear away the
bushes from around my tent. I now discovered that the
natives had been concealed behind a large tea-tree not
twenty yards from the tent: there were numerous foot-
marks there, and the remains of fire-sticks which they had
brought with them, for a native rarely moves at night with-
out fire."
Mr Eyre seems to have no hope, in spite of
Capt. Sturt's cheering dispatches, that any inland
sea will ever be ultimately discovered behind this
vast unpromising table land. Can it be, he asks,
that the whole is one immense interminable desert,
"or an alternation of deserts and shallow lakes? "
Incidental to the narrative of the expeditions
are many illustrations of native character: but Mr
Eyre, as we before said, has collected all his many
years' experiences on this head into a separate
treatise or dissertation at the close of his work.
The reader interested in the subject will find his
information curious and ample. The matters
treated of embrace not only the physical and moral
state of the aborigines; their habits of life, rude
government, and social relations; their language
and dialects; but also very interesting notices of
the effects of their contact with Europeans, and
some valuable suggestions for an improvement in
the system generally adopted towards them.
Our extracts are limited by our space: but to
even readers familiar with Captain Grey's excellent
dissertations, much of Mr Eyre's information will
be new and original.
HUSBAND AND WIFE.
" Wives are considered the absolute property of the hus-
band, and can be given away, or exchanged, or lent, ac-
cording to his caprice. A husband is denominated in the
Adelaide dialect, Yongarra, Martanya (the owner or pro-
prietor of a wife). Female children are betrothed usually
from early infancy, and such arrangements are usually ad-
hered to; still in many cases circumstances occur frequently
to cause an alteration; but if not, the girls generally go to
live with their husbands about the age of twelve, and some-
times even before that. Relatives nearer than cousins are
not allowed to marry, and this alliance does not generally
take place. Female orphans belong to the nearest male re-
lative, as also does a widow, instead of to the nearest male
relative of the husband, as was found to be the case in
Western Australia by Captain Grey. Two or three months
generally elapse before the widow goes to another hus-
band; but if the wife dies, the man takes another as soon
as he can get one. If a woman, having young children,
join another tribe, the children go with her; but I am not
aware whether they would remain permanently attached to
that tribe or not. Brothers often barter their sisters for
wives for themselves, but it can only be done with the
parents' consent, or after their death. If a wife be stolen,
war is always continued until she is given up, or another
female in her place.
"There is no ceremony connected with the undertaking
of marriage. In those cases where I have witnessed the
giving away of a wife, the woman was simply ordered by
the nearest male relative in whose disposal she was, to take
up her 'rocko,' the bag in which a female carries the effects
of her husband, and go to the man's camp to whom she had
been given. Marriage is not looked upon as any pledge of
chastity, indeed no such virtue is recognised. But little
real affection consequently exists between husbands and
wives, and young men value a wife principally for her ser-
vices as a slave; in fact, when asked why they are anxious
to obtain wives, their usual reply is, that they may get
wood, water, and food for them, and carry whatever pro-
perty they possess."
NATIVE MODESTY.
" Innate propriety of behaviour is also frequently exhi-
bited by the Aborigines in their natural state, in the modest
unassuming manner in which they take their positions to
observe what is going on, and in a total absence of any-
thing that is rude or offensive. It is true that the reverse
of this is also often to be met with; but I think it will
usually be found that it is among natives who have before
been in contact with Europeans, or where familiarities have
been used with them first, or an injudicious system of treat-
ment has been adopted towards them.
" Delicacy of feeling is not often laid to the charge of the
Aborigines, and yet I was witness to a singular instance of
it at King George's Sound. I was looking one evening at
the natives dancing, and who were, as they always are on
these occasions, in a state of complete nudity. In the
midst of the performance, one of the natives standing by as
a spectator, mentioned that a white woman was passing up
the road; and although this was some little distance away,
and the night was tolerably dark, they all with one accord
crossed over to the bushes where their cloaks were, put
them on, and resumed their amusement. "
Some representations of native ornaments, wea-
pons, and implements and works of industry, in
this part of the book, are useful to the text.
FOREIGN NEWS.
FRANCE.
DEATH OF M. ROYER COLLARD.—This illustrious
citizen died on the 4th inst., at his estate at Chateauneuf,
near Saint-Aignan, in the 82nd year of his age. M.
Royer Collard had been President of the Chamber of De-
puties, Member of the French Academy, and Professor of
Philosophy at the College of France.
THE SLAVE TRADE CONVENTION.—"The vessels in-
tended to act against the slave trade are not," says the
"Constitutionnel," "yet ready to proceed to the coasts of
Africa. They are not to set out for six weeks or two
months. Meanwhile communications are exchanged with
England every day on the subject of the mission which
the two navies are to fulfil together. Recently the Ad-
miralty has drawn up regulations for day and night sig-
nals, which the English and French cruisers are to make
use of, in order to mutually recognise each other. It ap-
pears that we have approved of all the dispositions of
these regulations. It is divided into two parts: the first
concerning sailing vessels, and the other steamers. The
English navy has been long occupied for its own use with
a regulation of this kind for steamers, collisions of which
are both frequent and dangerous. In France, nothing
has been done in that respect."
RUMOURED RETIREMENT OF MARSHAL SOULT.—A
letter from Castres announces that the Marquis de Mor-
nay has just arrived at Soulberg. If report can be be-
lieved, the marquis, who was at Beauvais for the Council-
General, quitted that town precipitately, in consequence
of a pressing invitation from the Minister of War. The
old marshal, who declares himself exceedingly fatigued
with the struggles and difficulties which he has to en-
counter, particularly from Algeria, and who is besides
tormented with a chronic cough, again talks of withdraw-
ing from office; but, as to withdraw at his age is to give
up public affairs for ever, he is unwilling, he says, to
take such a determination without consulting his family.
The 'France' discredits the report of the Marshal's
retirement.
VISIT OF THE FRENCH PRINCES TO THE QUEEN OF
SPAIN.—On the 3rd inst., the Duke and Duchess de Ne-
mours and the Duke d'Aumale, after visiting Biarritz
and St Jean de Luz, arrived at the bridge which unites
France with Spain. There the Princes alighted from
their carriages and crossed the bridge on foot, accompa-
nied by Count Bresson, the French Ambassador, the Pre-
fect of the Department of the Lower Pyrenees; M. Aze-
vedo; Gen. Boyer, Aid-de-Camp of the Duke de Ne-
mours; Col. Jamin, Aid-de-Camp of the Duke d'Aumale,
&c. On reaching the Spanish territory they were com-
plimented by the Duke de San Carlos, a nobleman of the
Queen's Bedchamber, and Senor Arana, Master of the
Ceremonies of the Palace, in the name of the Queen, and
by Senors Olozabal and Aldamar, in that of the province
of Guipuzcoa. Gen. Barrenechea, commander of the pro-
vince, received the French Princes at the head of the
troops with all the honours due to their rank. The people,
on their side, loudly cheered them. The august party
slept at Tolosa, and entered Pampeluna on the following
day. Accounts from Bayonne of the 8th state that they
had returned to that town in good health, highly satisfied
with the reception given them, not only at Pampeluna,
but along the whole of their journey in Spain. The Duke
d'Aumale travelled back through the valley of Bastan on
horseback.
FUTURE RESIDENCE OF DON CARLOS.—The 'Consti-
tutionnel' says:—" The Marquis de Villafranca is hourly
expected at Paris. He comes to solicit, it is said, autho-
risation for Don Carlos and the Princess to proceed to
Rome, the climate of Bourges being injurious to the health
of the Princess, who was born in Brazil. If M. de
Villafranca does not obtain passports for Italy, he is
directed to demand from the French Government per-
mission for Don Carlos and the Princess to fix their resi-
dence in such town of the south as they may choose."
THE POPE'S SENTIMENTS TOWARDS FRANCE.—The
"Journal des Debats" states that on the occasion of the
celebration of the fêtes of St Louis in the French church at
Rome, the Pope and a considerable number of cardinals
attended. M. Rossi, the French Plenipotentiary, opened
the door of the carriage at the church door, and thanked
his Holiness for the honour he had deigned to confer on the
French church. The Pope, in a voice so loud that he could
be heard by the crowd assembled around him, replied that
he had great pleasure in performing the pious duty, and
that he should be happy that that expression of his senti-
ments were known to the King of the French. After
prayers, his Holiness retired to an adjoining apartment,
where the ceremony of kissing his toe was gone through
by all the natives of France that presented themselves.
GERMANY.
RIOTS IN BRUNSWICK.—Advices from Brunswick of
the 3rd inst. state that during three consecutive evenings
joke of their own, which is much more remarkable
for its dullness than for any more lady-like quality.
LYCEUM.
An excellent new farce was played here on Mon-
day night; better than any piece of its class which
we have seen for many a day. It has nicety of
character, and a good broad humour. You laugh,
and have no need to be ashamed of your mirth.
There is neither caricature nor coarseness. We
cannot stay to tell the plot (which is a plot, and
not told without some pains), but must briefly
counsel the playgoer to see Peter Jenkins. Mr
and Mrs Keeley, Mr Wigan and Mr Meadows,
complete an admirable cast. Mr Keeley is not
only an honest truth-telling fellow forced to tell
lies for a friend; but a confirmed little bachelor,
caught, willy-nilly, in the snares of matrimony.
His dilemmas are intense, and he does justice to
them.
THE THEATRICAL EXAMINER.
HAYMARKET.
The False Mr Pope is a retired Hammersmith
tradesman of about five feet four, with a Ramilie
wig and tail more than half as big as himself,
square-cut buckram skirts, long flapped white
waistcoat, and minute three-cornered hat, who is
passed off by a wag of a player upon a party of
petticoat admirers of Pope, for the celebrated au-
thor of the Dunciad. To fancy Mr Buckstone in
this predicament, is to have a very clear notion of
Mr Peake's amusing farce.
It is nicely presented; with abundance of pe-
ruke for the gentlemen, and of hoods, clustering
curls, cardinals, and little china, for the ladies; and
it perpetrates a vast many abominable jokes, which
nobody but the actors and actresses can possibly
be expected to laugh at. But this is the "moral. " The
ladies are in such a state of frantic foregone
admiration of Mr Pope, that the more audacious
the flights of Mr Buckstone the wittier they are
taken to be; and though this is rather a danger-
ous experiment for a facce, the audience help it
ont with their good-nature.
Indeed it would take a troublesome amount of
the other quality to withstand Mr Buckstone's
practical points of drollery. When he takes off
his wig in a sudden heat, for example, and exposes
his small bald head, Swift's mouse under a canopy
of state is nothing to it. When he effects a series
of practical Rapes of the Loch, too, he uses the
scissors like a true poet. And when he passes
from doing to suffering, tastes the griefs as well as
glories of fame, and is well thrashed by Mr Curll's
chairman as he leaves the player's house, the act
closed with a roar. There should have been no
second. There is nothing but stale repetition in
the second act. The ladies retort with a practical
extract from the "Examiner" of Sept. 13, 1845.

        <Line>nan riktning. Gentemot pressens skar-</Line>
        <Line>pa yttranden öfwer Englands behand-</Line>
        <Line>lingssätt har regeringen konstaterat, att</Line>
        <Line>hennes press' deltagande är fremmande</Line>
        <Line>för denna riktning, och detta så mycket</Line>
        <Line>mera som man från intet håll åstundat</Line>
        <Line>att lära känna Tysklands omdöme öf-</Line>
        <Line>wer andra regeringars förfarande.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>London den 18 Juli, f. m. Mor-</Line>
        <Line>gonbladen tro, att utnämnandet af en</Line>
        <Line>efterträdare åt Bright skall leda till</Line>
        <Line>stora förändringar i kabinettet. — Ett</Line>
        <Line>telegram till Daily News från Alexan-</Line>
        <Line>dria meddelar: Från Kairo flydda per-</Line>
        <Line>soner berätta om mord på europeer i</Line>
        <Line>Tantåh, Mansnach och Zazazig. En</Line>
        <Line>konsul i Zazazig mördad.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Underhuset. Angående sina för-</Line>
        <Line>klaringar i underhuset sistl. onsdag och</Line>
        <Line>lördag förklarar Charles Dilke, att det</Line>
        <Line>kan förstås af sig sjelft, att brittiska</Line>
        <Line>regeringen icke begärt någon menings-</Line>
        <Line>yttring af fremmande regeringar öfwer</Line>
        <Line>en sådan punkt som Alexandrias bom-</Line>
        <Line>bardement. „Min förklaring", fortsät-</Line>
        <Line>ter Charles Dilke, „baserade sig i afse-</Line>
        <Line>ende å Österrike-Ungern dels å samtal</Line>
        <Line>mellan wårt sändebud i Wien, sir El-</Line>
        <Line>liot och grefwe Kalnoky och dels å</Line>
        <Line>samtal mellan det härwarande österri-</Line>
        <Line>kisk-ungerska sändebudet grefwe Karolui</Line>
        <Line>och lord Granville. I afseende å</Line>
        <Line>Tyskland finner jag nu, att det icke war</Line>
        <Line>berättigadt, då jag konstaterade, att ty-</Line>
        <Line>ska regeringen uttryckt sitt gonkännande</Line>
        <Line>af bombardementet; men i Onsdags och</Line>
        <Line>Lördags förefunnos de förhållanden,</Line>
        <Line>som öfwertygade mig att detta war fal-</Line>
        <Line>let." På en förfrågan af Cowen swa-</Line>
        <Line>rar Dilke, att det ännu ej finnes skrift-</Line>
        <Line>ligt swar på den identiska not, som i</Line>
        <Line>lördags öfwerräcktes åt Porten. —</Line>
        <Line>Machiwer frågar, om finanskontrollen</Line>
        <Line>i Egypten skall återställas och om den</Line>
        <Line>na sak förelegat konferensen till afgö-</Line>
        <Line>rande. Dilke swarar, att det i allmän-</Line>
        <Line>het är konferensens ändamål att åter-</Line>
        <Line>ställa de forna förhållandena i Egyp-</Line>
        <Line>ten; emellertid wore det omöjligt att nu</Line>
        <Line>redan omtala detaljerna af det framtida</Line>
        <Line>arrangementet. — På en förfrågan af</Line>
        <Line>Torrens swarar Dilke att tribunalerna</Line>
        <Line>i Alexandria äro räddade och nu skola</Line>
        <Line>besättas af en engelsk wakt. — Ami-</Line>
        <Line>ralitets-sekreteraren Bannermann med-</Line>
        <Line>delar huset: „Amiral Hoskins telegrafe-</Line>
        <Line>rar, att äfwen i Port Said tåder</Line>
        <Line>lugn."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Reuters Bureau förmäler från Ale-</Line>
        <Line>randria: Afsigten att besätta Ramleh</Line>
        <Line>uppgafs åter. Engelska auktoriteterna</Line>
        <Line>förklara att den engelska aktionens enda</Line>

        <Line>troserne skola i dag inställa tjensten till</Line>

        <Line>500 marinsoldater hålla sju punkter af</Line>
        <Line>staden besatta för att möjliggöra en</Line>
        <Line>werksam wakttjenst. Organisationen af</Line>
        <Line>en inhemsk polis har påbörjats. en-</Line>
        <Line>gelska patrullerna hafwa order att af-</Line>
        <Line>wäpna hwar och en, till och med Eu-</Line>
        <Line>ropeer, hwilka bära dolkar eller revolp-</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Konstantinopel d. 18: Por-</Line>

        <Line>Sändebuden skola förnya sin begäran.</Line>
        <Line>I går kallade sultanen det brittiska</Line>
